catalog_quote: In the Karelian language, every content word has stress. Stress is important as it forms the overall shape of the word and its boundaries. Karelian features dynamic word stress. ... Word stress in Karelian is constant. The primary stress always falls on the first syllable (pái-men / pái-moi ’a shepherd’), with the exception of some late Russian borrowings, in which the primary stress may sometimes fall on other syllables. In the standard varieties of Karelian stress can only be on the first syllable. The Karelian language always features secondary stress, which usually falls on every odd syllable of a compound noun, excluding the last one, while the second and even syllables remain unstressed (méč-čä-níek-ka / méč-čy-níek-ku ’a hunter’). A primary and secondary stress cannot, therefore, fall on consecutive syllables. ... The final syllable is usually unstressed. In dialects with apocope…

new_statements.quote: Word stress in Karelian is constant. The primary stress always falls on the first syllable (pái-men / pái-moi 'a shepherd'), with the exception of some late Russian borrowings, in which the primary stress may sometimes fall on other syllables. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress is fixed on the first syllable of the word in all Karelian varieties including Ludic; only some recent Russian loans may keep non-initial stress (and loans are normally adapted by moving stress to the first syllable, e.g. sámovuara < samovár).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on every odd-numbered syllable except the last; primary and secondary never adjacent; in apocopating dialects such as Ludic the (now) final syllable can retain secondary stress (méč-ník < méč-ník-ke); in compounds secondary stress on the first syllable of the second member.
new_statements.exceptions: Some late Russian borrowings may carry primary stress on a non-initial syllable; in connected speech stress may be lost or shift.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement for content words ('every content word has stress'); dynamic stress without vowel reduction; statement is made for Karelian as a whole (Karelian Proper, Livvi, Ludic) with a Ludic-specific example, synthesized from 21 grammars incl. three Ludic ones (Genetz 1872, Barantsev 1985 ms., Virtaranta 1986) and citing Barantsev 1975: 197.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is made for 'Karelian' in the Russian/KarRC sense, which treats Ludic (ludi1246) as one of three main dialects alongside Karelian Proper (kare1335) and Livvi (livv1243); the chapter gives a Ludic-specific example (méč-ník) and cites Barantsev 1975: 197 (Svyatozero = South Ludic). The Ludic grammars underlying the study are Genetz 1872 (North/Central Ludic), Barantsev 1985 ms. (Svyatozero, South Ludic) and Virtaranta 1986 (Haljärvi, North Ludic). Mikhailovskoye (Kuujärvi) Ludic is treated as a Ludic subdialect in the same work.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (initial stress = initial primary stress) and as the existing statement, which is this same passage (p. 81) in truncated form. Adds what the catalog does not record: alternating secondary stress on odd syllables, the Ludic apocope case where the final syllable keeps secondary stress (méč-ník), compound stress, and the Russian-loan exception. Note on identity of the item: the open copy at the listed URL is the 2022 English edition 'Karelian in Grammars' of the 2019 Russian study (p. 13 states it is the English edition of Karel'skij jazyk v grammatikah, KNC RAN 2019, with authors' corrections), not the Russian text itself; the statement is made for Karelian…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the first syllable of every content word (dynamic stress, no vowel reduction); only some late Russian loans may keep non-initial stress, and in the standard varieties stress is exclusively initial. In Russian loans the stress otherwise moves to the first syllable and the Russian stressed vowel is replaced by a long vowel or diphthong (sámovuara < samovár). Compounds: primary on the first syllable of the first member, secondary on the first syllable of the second member (pý-hä|pä́i-vä 'Sunday').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on every odd syllable (3rd, 5th..) excluding the final syllable; primary and secondary never on adjacent syllables; final syllable usually unstressed. Ludic-specific point: because Ludic has apocope, the syllables carrying primary and secondary stress have moved closer together, so the last syllable can retain a secondary stress (Ludic méč-ník / méč-ník-ke 'hunter'). In compounds the secondary stress falls on the first syllable of the second component. The page cites Barantsev 1975: 197 as the Ludic source (not obtainable online).
new_statements.exceptions: Some late Russian borrowings may carry primary stress on a non-initial syllable; in spoken dialects stress 'may be lost or it may move in the speech stream'.
new_statements.identity_note: The work treats Ludic as one of the three main dialects of Karelian (with Karelian Proper and Livvi-Karelian) and its stress chapter is written for Karelian generally, with Ludic represented by three descriptions: Barantsev 1985 ms. (Svyatozero subdialect, South Ludic), Genetz 1872 (northern Ludic) and Virtaranta 1986 (Haljärvi/Gallezero, Central Ludic); the Ludic stress source cited on p. 81 is Barantsev 1975: 197 (Svyatozero). The Ludic-specific example méč-ník / méč-ník-ke illustrates apocope dialects. The listed citation is the 2019 Russian original; the open copy is the 2022 English edition of the same study (p. 13 'Reader's Aid'), which the authors say incorporates corrections to the Russian, Finnish and Karelian editions.

sources.note: Ch. 6 'Word stress', p. 81: Karelian (Karelian Proper, Livvi, Ludic) has dynamic, constant word stress; primary stress always on the first syllable except some late Russian loans; secondary stress on odd non-final syllables; in apocopating dialects the final syllable may keep secondary stress (Ludic example méč-ník / méč-ník-ke); compounds: primary on first syllable of first member, secondary on first syllable of second member. Cites Barantsev 1975: 197 among others.
